story.text: Reuben lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine, “and Israel heard it”.
He talked his brothers out of killing Joseph, meaning to bring him back to his father.
Dathan, Abiram and On, “sons of Reuben”, joined Korah's rebellion against Moses and Aaron.
Reuben and Gad, rich in cattle, asked for the land east of the Jordan rather than a share in Canaan.
With Gad and half of Manasseh they built a great altar by the Jordan; the other tribes gathered at Shiloh to go to war over it, and it was named Ed, “a witness”.
Deborah's song reproaches Reuben for staying “among the sheepfolds”.
Chronicles explains that Reuben's birthright passed to Joseph's sons because “he defiled his father's bed”.

fate.text: He carried away “the Reubenites, and the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh” to Halah, Habor, Hara and the river Gozan.
Samaria fell and Israel was carried away into Assyria; “there was none left but the tribe of Judah only”.

O my soul, come not thou into their secret; unto their assembly, mine honour, be not thou united: for in their anger they slew a man, and in their selfwill they digged down a wall. moses.text: And of Levi he said, Let thy Thummim and thy Urim be with thy holy one, whom thou didst prove at Massah, and with whom thou didst strive at the waters of Meribah; Who said unto his father and to his mother, I have not seen him; neither did he acknowledge his brethren, nor knew his own children: for they have observed thy word, and kept thy covenant. They shall teach Jacob thy judgments, and Israel thy law: they shall put incense before thee, and whole burnt sacrifice upon thine altar. Bless, LORD, his substance, and accept the work of his hands: smite through the loins of them that rise against him, and of them that hate him, that they rise not again.

blessings.note: Jacob's words (Genesis 49:5–7) are spoken to Simeon and Levi together; Moses blesses Levi alone, and at length (Deuteronomy 33:8–11).

change.note: Our own arithmetic: the second figure minus the first.

census.note: Levi was not numbered with the tribes (Numbers 1:47–49). It was counted apart, every male “from a month old and upward”: 22,000 (Numbers 3:39) and 23,000 (Numbers 26:62). The three clan counts in Numbers 3 (7,500, 8,600 and 6,200; verses 22, 28, 34) add up to 22,300 by our own arithmetic, 300 more than the total the text gives.
census.basis: males from a month old and upward

camp.note: The Levites camp around the tabernacle in the midst of the four camps (Numbers 1:53; 2:17), clan by clan (Numbers 3:23–38).

prince.note: Levi has no prince in Numbers 1. Numbers 3 names a chief for each Levite clan: Eliasaph the son of Lael (Gershonites, 3:24), Elizaphan the son of Uzziel (Kohathites, 3:30), Zuriel the son of Abihail (Merarites, 3:35), with Eleazar the son of Aaron “chief over the chief of the Levites” (3:32).

spy.note: Levi sent no spy: the twelve in Numbers 13:4–15 are the other tribes, with Joseph counted as Ephraim and Manasseh.

levitical.family: the rest of the Kohathites (west half of Manasseh)

land.note: Levi received no territory: “the LORD God of Israel was their inheritance” (Joshua 13:33). Its share was forty-eight cities with their suburbs inside the other tribes (Joshua 21:41).

story.text: Levi joined Simeon when they came upon Shechem “and slew all the males”.
When Moses asked “Who is on the LORD's side?” after the golden calf, “all the sons of Levi” came to him.
The Levites were taken in place of Israel's firstborn and set over the tabernacle.
Levi received no land: the LORD was their inheritance, and they were given forty-eight cities among the other tribes.
When Jeroboam cast them out of the priesthood, the Levites of the north left their towns and came to Judah and Jerusalem.

fate.text: The priests and the Levites returned with Judah and Benjamin.
The Levites of the north had already moved to Judah in Rehoboam's time.
At the dedication of the rebuilt temple, twelve goats were offered “according to the number of the tribes of Israel”.

nt.text: Barnabas was “a Levite, and of the country of Cyprus”.

Hebrews contrasts Levi's priesthood with one from Judah, “of which tribe Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood”.

ezekiel.note: Levi has no band: the Levites' land lies within the holy portion (48:13). Levi has a gate on the north (48:31).

story.text: The Amorites forced Dan into the hills and would not let it come down to the valley.
Deborah's song asks “why did Dan remain in ships?”
Samson, the son of Manoah of the Danites, judged Israel.
Dan, whose inheritance “had not fallen unto them”, sent five men to spy out the land, then took Laish, renamed it Dan, and set up a graven image with its own priests.
Jeroboam put one of his two golden calves at Dan.
The whole of Israel gathered “from Dan even to Beer-sheba”, a phrase for the land from north to south.

fate.text: Samaria fell and Israel was carried away into Assyria; “there was none left but the tribe of Judah only”.

lists.notes: The family that went down to Egypt, by mother, now Leah, Zilpah, Rachel, Bilhah. Joseph's sons Manasseh and Ephraim are named as born in Egypt (46:20).

lists.label: Jacob's blessing
lists.notes: Simeon and Levi share one saying (49:5–7). Zebulun comes before his elder brother Issachar. The text closes: “All these are the twelve tribes of Israel” (49:28).

lists.label: The names in Egypt
lists.notes: Eleven names: Joseph is left out of the list “for Joseph was in Egypt already” (1:5).

lists.label: The princes who helped number Israel
lists.notes: Levi is left out and Joseph is split into Ephraim and Manasseh (“Of the children of Joseph”, 1:10), keeping the count at twelve.

lists.label: The first census
lists.notes: Gad moves up to third, the place Levi had: the order now matches the camps of Numbers 2 by threes. “The Levites … were not numbered among them” (1:47).

lists.label: The camp around the tabernacle
lists.notes: Four camps of three, each under a standard: Judah east, Reuben south, Ephraim west, Dan north. The Levites camp “in the midst” (2:17).

lists.label: Twelve days of offerings
lists.notes: One prince a day for twelve days, in the order of the camp. Every prince brings the same offering, and the text repeats it in full each day.

lists.label: Breaking camp
lists.notes: The camp order on the march. The Levites are split: Gershon and Merari carry the tabernacle after Judah's camp (10:17), the Kohathites carry the sanctuary after Reuben's (10:21). Dan is “the rereward of all the camps” (10:25).

lists.label: The twelve spies
lists.notes: A different order again: Ephraim and Manasseh are separated by Benjamin and Zebulun, and Manasseh is called “the tribe of Joseph” (13:11). Gad comes last.

lists.label: The second census
lists.notes: The order of Numbers 1, except that Manasseh now comes before Ephraim. Levi is counted apart afterwards (26:57–62).

lists.label: The men who divided the land
lists.notes: Ten tribes only: Reuben and Gad (and half of Manasseh) had already received land east of the Jordan (34:14–15), and Levi received none. The order runs roughly from south to north, as the land was later allotted, though this reading of the order is our own observation.

lists.label: Gerizim and Ebal
lists.notes: Six on each mountain. On Gerizim stand four of Leah's sons and both of Rachel's; on Ebal, Leah's eldest and youngest with the four sons of the handmaids (our own observation from Genesis 35:23–26). Levi and Joseph are each one tribe here.

lists.label: Moses' blessing
lists.notes: Eleven blessings: Simeon is not named. Ephraim and Manasseh appear inside Joseph's blessing (33:17).

lists.label: The land allotted
lists.notes: East of the Jordan first, given by Moses (Reuben, Gad, half Manasseh), then Judah and Joseph's two tribes, then seven lots cast at Shiloh (18:10), from Benjamin to Dan. Manasseh appears twice, once for each half. Levi has no land (13:14, 33).

lists.label: Where the Levites' cities came from

cells.asNamed: half tribe of Manasseh in Bashan

lists.notes: Levi is the receiver here, not a giver. Manasseh appears twice (each half gives cities).

lists.label: Deborah's song
lists.notes: The song praises six and reproaches four. Judah, Simeon and Levi are not mentioned at all. “Machir” (Manasseh's son, Numbers 26:29) stands for Manasseh; “Gilead … beyond Jordan” is read as Gad (and eastern Manasseh) by many commentators, a reading, not the text.

lists.label: The sons of Israel
lists.notes: Leah's six, then Dan placed between Zebulun and Joseph, ahead of the other handmaids' sons: an order found nowhere else.

lists.label: The genealogies of Chronicles
lists.notes: Judah first and longest (2:3–4:23). Dan and Zebulun have no genealogy. Benjamin is given twice (7:6–12 and all of chapter 8). Naphtali gets one verse (7:13).

lists.label: Who came to make David king
lists.notes: The armed men who came to Hebron. Every tribe appears, Levi included, with Joseph as Ephraim and two halves of Manasseh. The tribes east of the Jordan are counted together (120,000, 12:37).

lists.label: David's rulers of the tribes

cells.asNamed: half tribe of Manasseh in Gilead

lists.notes: Gad and Asher are missing. Levi has a ruler and so do “the Aaronites” (Zadok, 27:17), and Manasseh has two: thirteen rulers in all (our own count).

lists.label: Ezekiel's portions
lists.notes: Twelve bands from north to south, seven above the holy portion (48:8–22) and five below. Levi has no band: the Levites' land is inside the holy portion (48:13). “Joseph shall have two portions” (47:13).

lists.label: The gates of Ezekiel's city
lists.notes: In the same chapter the list changes: the gates are named for Levi and for Joseph as one tribe, so Ephraim and Manasseh drop out.

lists.label: The sealed of Revelation
lists.notes: Twelve thousand sealed from each of twelve tribes (144,000, 7:4). Judah comes first. Dan and Ephraim are absent; Levi is counted; Joseph and Manasseh both appear, so Joseph's line is in effect named twice (our own observation).

kingdom.northNote: Our inference: the text gives the north “ten tribes” but never lists them by name. Simeon lived inside Judah (Joshua 19:1) yet is later named with Ephraim and Manasseh (2 Chronicles 15:9); the Levites of the north moved south (2 Chronicles 11:13–14).

claims.text: Ahijah tore his new garment into twelve pieces and told Jeroboam to take ten: “I will … give ten tribes to thee”.
Solomon's son was to keep “one tribe for my servant David's sake, and for Jerusalem's sake”.
When Israel made Jeroboam king, “there was none that followed the house of David, but the tribe of Judah only”.
Yet the next verse has Rehoboam gather “all the house of Judah, with the tribe of Benjamin”, and Chronicles says he had “Judah and Benjamin on his side”.
So the text counts ten and one, then names two in the south. Ten and one make eleven of twelve: how Benjamin, Simeon and Levi fit the count is not stated (our own observation).
The priests and Levites throughout Israel came over to Rehoboam, and after them people “out of all the tribes of Israel” who sought the LORD.
Ezekiel is told to join “the stick of Joseph, which is in the hand of Ephraim” with “the stick of Judah” into one.

views.question: Why is Dan missing from the sealed tribes of Revelation 7?
views.order: in the order the views arose

facts.text: Revelation 7:5–8 names twelve tribes with twelve thousand sealed from each; Dan is not among them, and neither is Ephraim, while Levi and Joseph are.

views.label: The Antichrist would come from Dan
views.holders: Irenaeus (about AD 180); later Bede and Andreas, as the Pulpit Commentary reports

argument.text: Irenaeus links Jeremiah's words about Dan with the coming of the Antichrist, and says this is “the reason that this tribe is not reckoned in the Apocalypse along with those which are saved”.

views.label: Dan was left out for its idolatry
views.holders: Hengstenberg and Wordsworth, as the Pulpit Commentary reports; Barnes (1851) records it as the view of “some”

argument.text: The Danites set up a graven image with their own priesthood (Judges 18:30), and Jeroboam put one of his golden calves at Dan (1 Kings 12:29).

views.label: A copyist's slip
views.holders: Heinrich Ewald, as the Pulpit Commentary reports

argument.text: Ewald proposed that John wrote “Dan” (ΔΑΝ) and that a copyist read it as “Man.”, short for Manasses, so that Manasseh displaced Dan.

facts.text: Simeon's cities lay “within the inheritance of the children of Judah” (Joshua 19:1, 9); the tribe has no blessing in Deuteronomy 33 and its census falls from 59,300 to 22,200 (Numbers 1:23; 26:14).

views.label: Absorbed into Judah
views.holders: International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, “Simeon (1)” (1915); Keil and Delitzsch on Genesis 49:7 (1861)

argument.text: Simeon received no territory of its own, only cities inside Judah, and those cities are also listed as Judah's (Joshua 15:26–32). 1 Chronicles 4:31 says “These were their cities unto the reign of David”. ISBE writes of Simeon's dependence on Judah and its final absorption into it.

views.label: Partly scattered, and counted with the north
views.holders: International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915), noting the later references; the Pulpit Commentary on Joshua 19:9, on the Simeonites at mount Seir

argument.text: Some Simeonites moved to new pasture and to mount Seir in Hezekiah's days (1 Chronicles 4:41–43), and Chronicles names Simeon beside Ephraim and Manasseh, among those who came over from the northern kingdom (2 Chronicles 15:9; 34:6).

views.question: Were the ten northern tribes lost?
views.order: in the order the views arose

facts.text: Assyria carried the northern tribes away (2 Kings 15:29; 17:6; 1 Chronicles 5:26) and “there was none left but the tribe of Judah only” (2 Kings 17:18); yet Chronicles later names people of Ephraim, Manasseh, Asher, Issachar and Zebulun at Hezekiah's passover (2 Chronicles 30:11, 18), and the New Testament speaks of “our twelve tribes” (Acts 26:7).

views.label: They live on, apart, beyond the Euphrates
views.holders: Josephus (about AD 93); the apocalypse 2 Esdras 13 (late first century AD), as the Jewish Encyclopedia (1906) sets out

argument.text: Josephus writes that “the ten tribes are beyond Euphrates till now; and are an immense multitude”. 2 Esdras 13:40–45 tells of the ten tribes travelling a year and a half to a land called Arsareth.

views.label: They will never return
views.holders: Rabbi Akiba (early second century AD), Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:3, as the Jewish Encyclopedia (1906) reports

argument.text: Akiba held that the ten tribes would not come back.

views.label: Never lost: Israel still counted twelve tribes
views.holders: Joseph Benson (1811–1818), E. H. Plumptre in the Cambridge Bible (1878), the Pulpit Commentary, all on James 1:1

argument.text: James writes “to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad”, Paul speaks of “our twelve tribes”, and Anna is “of the tribe of Aser”: these commentators read the northern tribes as still present among the Jews of the first century.

views.question: What does “until Shiloh come” mean (Genesis 49:10)?
views.order: most widely held first among the commentaries cited

facts.text: Jacob says “The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come”.

views.label: A name of the Messiah, “the peaceful one”

argument.text: Shiloh is read as a title from a Hebrew root meaning rest or peace, pointing to a coming ruler of peace from Judah.

views.label: “He whose it is”
views.holders: the ancient versions (the Greek Septuagint; the Aramaic Targum Onkelos, “until Messiah come, whose is the kingdom”, as Ellicott quotes it); H. E. Ryle in the Cambridge Bible (1914), who calls it the most probable reading

argument.text: Read as “shelloh”, the words mean “until he come whose it is”, that is, the one to whom the sceptre belongs.

views.question: Why do Dan and Zebulun have no genealogy in 1 Chronicles 2–8?
views.order: in the order of the sources

facts.text: The genealogies of 1 Chronicles 2–8 give every tribe except Dan and Zebulun; 1 Chronicles 7:12 ends Benjamin's list with “Hushim, the sons of Aher”, and Genesis 46:23 names Dan's only son Hushim.

views.label: Dan is hidden in 1 Chronicles 7:12
views.holders: W. E. Barnes in the Cambridge Bible (1899)

argument.text: “Aher” (“another”) may stand where Dan's name once stood, so that “Hushim” is Dan's family.
Zebulun is left out as well, so the omissions are taken as accidents of the record, not as a judgment on Dan.

traditionNotes.text: Exodus says the breastplate stones bore the names of the children of Israel, “according to the twelve tribes”, but does not say which name went on which stone.

Josephus lists the stones in four rows of three: sardonyx, topaz, emerald; carbuncle, jasper, sapphire; ligure, amethyst, agate; chrysolite, onyx, beryl. His order and his names for the stones differ from the KJV of Exodus 28:17–20.

The midrash on Numbers 2:2 (“every man … by his own standard, with the ensign of their father's house”) gives each tribe a colour and an emblem matched to a breastplate stone. Its stone order follows Exodus 28:17–20 with the tribes in the order Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Dan, Gad, Naphtali, Asher, Joseph, Benjamin.
